01 / THE PROJECT

Start with dependable data.

Spendwise is an ongoing Java and Spring Boot project focused on the backend of a personal finance tracker. The public version supports creating transactions, retrieving the full collection, and looking up an individual transaction. It separates the API, business logic, and data access so each part has a clear responsibility.

The problem

Tracking spending starts with dependable records. A merchant, amount, date, category, and transaction type need a consistent structure before they can support useful financial summaries. This project starts with that foundation and uses Postman to work directly with the API while the backend develops.

JSON request bodyIllustrative request · no live API

What’s implemented

Transaction endpoints
Create a transaction, list all transactions, and retrieve one by ID through /api/transactions.
Input validation
Require a merchant, positive amount, date, category, and transaction type before saving.
Clear error responses
Return validation errors for individual fields with HTTP 400, and HTTP 404 when a requested transaction is missing.
Separated persistence
Use a Spring Data JPA repository and a Transaction entity for database access, with PostgreSQL integration.

02 / HOW IT FITS TOGETHER

Clear responsibilities.

Technology choices

Java + Spring Boot
Define typed transaction data and HTTP endpoints with a familiar application structure.
Spring Data JPA + PostgreSQL
Keep database operations behind a repository instead of embedding queries in the controller.
BigDecimal + LocalDate
Represent decimal transaction amounts and dates explicitly in the data model.
Maven + Postman
Manage project dependencies and exercise the API during development.

03 / ENGINEERING DECISIONS

The interesting parts.

01

Make invalid data useful to the caller.

An incomplete transaction should produce an actionable response. The model uses validation annotations, the controller applies @Valid, and a shared exception handler turns field errors into a response keyed by field name. A missing merchant can therefore be reported directly instead of becoming an unexplained server failure.

The tradeoff

Returning the entity directly keeps this early API small. A separate request/response model would give future versions more control over what callers can submit and receive.

02

Keep the route separate from the work.

TransactionController delegates to TransactionService, which uses TransactionRepository. When an ID is missing, the service raises NotFoundException and the shared handler produces a 404. The same error policy can apply without duplicating response logic in every endpoint.

The tradeoff

The service layer is deliberately thin at this stage. It provides a place for future rules without adding those rules before they are needed.

04 / TESTING & EVIDENCE

What the evidence supports.

API development has been checked manually through Postman. The inspected public repository includes a test that loads the Spring application context, but does not yet contain endpoint or validation regression tests. The API example is an illustrative request based on the current model; it is not a captured live response.

05 / REFLECTION

Lessons and what comes next.

A small API makes the boundaries visible: the controller handles requests, the service coordinates behavior, and the repository handles storage. Validation and centralized errors give that structure a consistent contract for callers.

Current limitations

The published version focuses on create and read operations. A frontend and broader budgeting features remain future work. Update/delete and CSV preview are not part of this public source snapshot.

Next engineering steps

  • Add endpoint and validation regression tests.
  • Publish and verify the remaining transaction and CSV preview work.
  • Build financial summaries on top of the transaction model.
